t.5.14.1: Having praised Sītā, who was worthy of praise, and Rāma, delightful in his virtues, that bull among monkeys became once more absorbed in thought.
t.5.14.2: Having reflected for what seemed but a moment, his eyes brimming with tears, the radiant Hanumān, his thoughts fixed on Sītā, lamented.
t.5.14.3: If even Sītā, who is worthy of reverence from Lakṣmaṇa, disciplined by his elders, and who is dear to his elder brother, is stricken with sorrow, then Time is indeed hard to overcome.
t.5.14.4: Knowing the resolve of Rāma and of wise Lakṣmaṇa, the queen is not greatly agitated, like the Gaṅgā at the coming of the rain-clouds.
t.5.14.5: Rāghava is worthy of Vaidehī, who is equal to him in character, age and conduct, equal in lineage and auspicious marks; and she, the dark-eyed one, is worthy of him.
t.5.14.6: Seeing her, radiant like new gold and like Śrī herself beloved of the world, he went in his mind to Rāma and spoke these words.
t.5.14.7: It was for the sake of this large-eyed lady that the mighty Vālī, a match for Rāvaṇa in valor, was slain, and Kabandha too was struck down.
t.5.14.8: And in the forest Rāma, with a mighty onslaught, slew in battle the rākṣasa Virādha of fearsome valour, as Mahendra slew Śambara.
t.5.14.9: Fourteen thousand rākṣasas of terrible deeds were slain in Janasthāna by arrows resembling tongues of fire.
t.5.14.10: Khara was slain in battle, and Triśiras was struck down, as was the greatly mighty Dūṣaṇa, by Rāma, whose self is well known.
t.5.14.11: And for her sake Sugrīva obtained the sovereignty over the monkeys, hard to attain, once guarded by Vālin and honored by the world.
t.5.14.12: For the sake of this large-eyed lady I have crossed the glorious ocean, lord of rivers and streams, and searched through this city as well.
t.5.14.14: Weigh sovereignty over the three worlds against Sītā, the daughter of Janaka: the entire kingdom of the three worlds would not equal even a fraction of Sītā.
t.5.14.13: If Rāma were to overturn the sea-bounded earth for her sake, and even the whole world, it would be fitting; such is my opinion.
t.5.14.15: This is that Sītā, daughter of King Janaka, the high-souled lord of Mithilā whose nature is devoted to dharma, she who is firm in her vow of devotion to her husband.
t.5.14.17: This is the illustrious eldest daughter-in-law of King Daśaratha, the valiant one of noble character who never turned back in battles.
t.5.14.16: Rising up after splitting the earth in a field furrowed by the tip of the plough, she was covered with the auspicious dust of the field, which looked like lotus pollen.
t.5.14.18: This is she, the beloved wife of Rāma, who knows dharma, who is grateful and whose self is known, now fallen into the power of rākṣasīs.
t.5.14.20: She who, content with fruits and roots and devoted to serving her husband, enjoys supreme happiness even in the forest, just as she would in a palace.
t.5.14.19: Abandoning all comforts, driven by the strength of her love for her husband, and giving no thought to hardships, she entered the desolate forest.
t.5.14.21: This very lady, whose limbs are the color of gold and who always speaks with a gentle smile, endures this torment, though she has no share in misfortunes.
t.5.14.22: Rāghava longs to see her, this woman endowed with virtuous character, carried off by Rāvaṇa, just as a thirsty man longs to see a wayside watering-place that has been laid waste.
t.5.14.24: Abandoned by the pleasures of love and bereft of her kinsfolk, she sustains her own body, longing for reunion with him.
t.5.14.23: Surely, on regaining her, Rāghava will attain joy, like a king fallen from his kingdom who wins back the earth once more.
t.5.14.25: She sees neither the rākṣasīs nor these trees laden with flowers and fruit; with her heart fixed on one thing alone, surely she beholds only Rāma.
t.5.14.26: A husband, indeed, is a woman's supreme ornament, greater even than any ornament; for this lady, though worthy of splendor, does not shine, being deprived of him.
t.5.14.27: Lord Rāma does a thing most difficult to do, in that, bereft of her, he still sustains his own body and does not sink down under his sorrow.
t.5.14.28: Seeing her, with the ends of her hair so dark and her eyes like hundred-petalled lotuses, she who deserves happiness yet is sunk in sorrow, even my mind is pained.
t.5.14.30: Like a lotus pond struck by frost, her beauty lost, oppressed by a succession of calamities, like a cakravākī bereft of her mate, the daughter of Janaka had fallen into a pitiable state.
t.5.14.29: She who is patient as the earth, whose eyes are like lotuses, and who was once protected by Rāghava and Lakṣmaṇa, is now guarded at the foot of a tree by rākṣasīs with hideous eyes.
t.5.14.32: Having thus considered the matter, the monkey, his mind firmly settled on the thought "This is Sītā," took refuge in that tree and sat down there, the mighty and swift bull among the monkeys.
t.5.14.31: For her, the aśoka trees, the tips of their branches bowed down with blossoms, surely awaken deep sorrow; and with the passing of winter, the sun, whose rays had been feeble, has risen blazing with many thousands of rays.
